faq.q: Why do I yawn when someone else yawns?
faq.a: Seeing a yawn activates brain areas involved in copying actions, which can trigger your own yawn. Scientists are still working out the full reason, but it seems linked to how social brains respond to others.

faq.q: Do we catch yawns more from friends?
faq.a: Yes. Several studies found people catch yawns most from close family, then friends, and least from strangers. This is one reason scientists link it to social bonds and empathy.
asks: Are yawns more catching from family?

faq.q: Can reading about yawns make you yawn?
faq.a: Yes. Seeing, hearing, reading or even thinking about yawning can be enough to trigger a yawn, because each reminds the brain of the action.
asks: Why do I yawn reading about yawning?
Can hearing a yawn make you yawn?

faq.q: Why do we yawn at all?
faq.a: Nobody knows for sure. A leading idea is that the deep breath and jaw stretch help cool the brain; others say yawns help us change between states, like sleepy to alert. The old idea that yawns fix low oxygen has not held up in experiments.
asks: What is the purpose of yawning?
Do we yawn because we need oxygen?

faq.a: Chimpanzees and bonobos catch yawns from each other, and some studies suggest dogs can catch yawns from people they know. Babies and toddlers rarely catch yawns; it usually starts at around four or five years old.
asks: Can dogs catch yawns from people?

facts: Contagious yawning usually does not appear in children until about four or five years old.
Experiments have shown that breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning, which argues against the low-oxygen explanation.
